lesson.title: Always True: When Every Number Works
lesson.summary: Learn to recognize an identity, an equation that is true for every value of the variable, and see why the variable disappears into a true numerical statement when solved.
lesson.body:
An identity equation is a linear equation in one variable that is true for absolutely every value that could be substituted in, because the two sides are actually the same expression, just written differently. When you try to solve one using the usual steps, gathering variable terms on one side and constants on the other, the variable terms cancel out completely, and what remains is a true numerical statement, such as 6 = 6 or 0 = 0. That outcome is not a mistake or a dead end; it is the equation telling you that its solution set is all real numbers.

Solve 3(2x - 4) = 6x - 12. Distribute the 3 on the left side: 6x - 12 = 6x - 12. Subtract 6x from both sides: -12 = -12. This is a true statement, and the variable x has completely disappeared from the equation; there was nothing wrong with the algebra, the two sides were equivalent all along, since 3(2x - 4) always equals 6x - 12 for any value of x. Testing this with a number confirms it: let x = 5, then the left side is 3(2(5) - 4) = 3(10 - 4) = 3(6) = 18, and the right side is 6(5) - 12 = 30 - 12 = 18, matching. Trying x = 0 also works: left side is 3(2(0) - 4) = 3(-4) = -12, and right side is 6(0) - 12 = -12, matching again.

A second example shows how an identity can hide behind combined like terms rather than only distribution. Consider 4(x + 2) - 3x = x + 8. Distribute the 4: 4x + 8 - 3x = x + 8. Combine like terms on the left: x + 8 = x + 8. Subtracting x from both sides gives 8 = 8, another true statement with the variable gone, confirming this is also an identity with a solution set of all real numbers, even though the two sides did not look identical before simplifying.

Identities arise because one side of the equation is an equivalent, rewritten form of the other, usually produced by distributing a factor across parentheses, combining like terms, or applying a property such as the distributive property. Recognizing this in advance is not required, since the solving process itself reveals an identity: if every variable term cancels and a true statement remains, the equation was an identity from the start, regardless of how complicated it initially looked.

This is exactly one of the three outcomes previewed when linear equations in one variable were introduced, and it corresponds to a solution set of all real numbers, as discussed with the solution set concept. It is worth pausing on this because it directly contradicts the common assumption that every equation has exactly one answer; an identity has infinitely many, since literally any real number can be substituted for x and the equation will still hold.

An identity is one extreme outcome; the opposite extreme, where the variable also disappears but leaves behind a false statement instead of a true one, is called a contradiction, examined next. Learning to tell the two apart quickly, both by the appearance of a numerical statement with no variable left, and by whether that statement is true or false, is the key skill tying this section to the next.
